_why:
Nullability that MEASUREMENT CANNOT SUPPLY, declared as data so it is visible instead of hand-edited into the generated file.

The engine emits no explicit null anywhere in the 746 measured artefacts, so every field measures as non-nullable. For most fields that is the right boundary. For the few fields the SUBJECT SUBSTITUTION rule reads, it is not: rejecting an artefact whose committed subject carries an explicit null kind makes the row unreadable, and an unreadable identity CAPS the verdict at agree_weak -- so a row that earns `disagree` as a substitution is upgraded by our own doubt. That is strictly worse than the malformed value it was meant to catch, and it is a bug this instrument has already shipped once.

So these paths ADMIT an explicit null and reject every other wrong type. `kind: []` and `kind: 1` are still rejected; `kind: null` reaches the substitution rule, which is the code that knows a null kind cannot satisfy a declared anchor. The policy is narrow on purpose: it names paths, not types, and every entry carries the consumer that depends on it.

The candidate mirror is listed too, and that is not padding: a malformed commit carries the same null in `candidates[].subject`, so admitting it on `committed[]` alone leaves the artefact rejected by the other path and the upgrade bug intact. Found by executing the null-kind row end to end rather than by reading the policy and assuming it covered the case -- the schema said ok and the ROW still scored agree_weak.

CHAOS-5430 r2, P2 from round 1: the candidate mirror is CONDITIONAL. Round 1 observed that an all-null UNCOMMITTED candidate also validated -- true, and wider than the substitution rule needs, since identity scoring only reads committed candidates. The mirror entries now carry a `when` clause and admit null only where the candidate's own `state` is `committed`. A proposed or ambiguous candidate with a null subject is rejected, as it was before the mirror was added.

CHAOS-5430 r3: a `when` clause NAMES ITS OBJECT -- `parent.state`, not `state` -- and there is no fallback. Round 2 found the fallback spoofable: the check looked in the immediate container first and only then at the parent, so a PROPOSED candidate carrying `subject.state="committed"` satisfied a clause meant to read the candidate's own state and got its null subject admitted. The fallback existed because I did not want to write down which object the clause refers to. A discriminator any nested object can satisfy is not a discriminator.

admit_null.consumer: subject_identity.anchor_satisfied -- a null kind must FAIL the anchor check, not skip it
subject_identity dedup key (kind, canonical_id) -- a null id is a distinct subject, not an unreadable artefact
subject_identity.anchor_satisfied -- a null label cannot correspond to a declared anchor NAME

subject_identity -- the committed candidate MIRRORS the committed subject; rejecting the mirror makes the artefact unreadable and re-upgrades the row the committed[] policy exists to keep at disagree -- CONDITIONAL on state=committed
subject_identity dedup key, via the candidate mirror -- CONDITIONAL on state=committed
subject_identity.anchor_satisfied, via the candidate mirror -- CONDITIONAL on state=committed
